title: Unified Osculator Theorem
description: Merges the positive and negative osculator theorems into a single unified theorem with a signed osculator c in Z. The negative osculator case is derived as a corollary by substituting -c, and a dual osculator relationship theorem shows that the sum of positive and negative osculators is divisible by d.

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules using "osculators" (multipliers applied to the last digit) have roots in Martin Gardner's recreational mathematics and earlier work by V. Ramaswami Aiyar (1907). The positive osculator test ($d | n \iff d | (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n \bmod 10))$ when $10c \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$) and the negative variant ($10c \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$) have traditionally been treated as separate rules. The parent formalization (divisibility-truncation-general) proved both cases independently, raising the natural question: can they be unified? This proof shows the answer is yes — the negative case is the positive case with $c$ negated, since $d | (10c_{\text{neg}} + 1)$ implies $d | (10(-c_{\text{neg}}) - 1)$. The unification reveals a deeper structure: positive and negative osculators are not independent constructions but additive inverses under the same modular arithmetic.
overview.problemStatement:
Can the positive and negative osculator theorems be merged into a single theorem with a signed osculator c in Z?

**Answer: YES.** The unified osculator theorem states: for any d coprime to 10 and any c in Z satisfying d | (10c - 1):

  d | n <-> d | (n/10 + c * (n%10))

The negative osculator case follows by substituting c = -c_neg, since d | (10*c_neg + 1) implies d | (10*(-c_neg) - 1).
overview.proofStrategy:
The unified theorem uses the same algebraic identity as the parent proof:

  10 * (n/10 + c*(n%10)) = n + (10c - 1)*(n%10)

When d | (10c - 1), the remainder term is divisible by d, and coprimality with 10 allows cancelling the factor of 10.

The negative case then follows by a simple sign flip: given d | (10*c_neg + 1), we show 10*(-c_neg) - 1 = -(10*c_neg + 1), so d | (10*(-c_neg) - 1). Applying the unified theorem with osculator -c_neg immediately yields the negative rule.

The dual osculator theorem observes that 10*c_pos - 1 + (10*c_neg + 1) = 10*(c_pos + c_neg), so d divides this sum, and coprimality gives d | (c_pos + c_neg).
keyInsights: The negative osculator case is not independent: it is the positive case with c negated.
Sign absorption: d | (10*c_neg + 1) iff d | (10*(-c_neg) - 1), reducing two theorems to one.
The dual osculator relationship (c_pos + c_neg divisible by d) follows from the sum of the two osculator conditions.
Lean's IsCoprime and linear_combination handle the algebraic manipulations cleanly.
All five classical divisibility rules (7, 11, 13, 17, 19) are recovered from the single unified theorem.

sections.title: The Unified Osculator Theorem
sections.summary: Single theorem: d | n <-> d | (n/10 + c*(n%10)) for any c with d | (10c - 1).
sections.mathContext: The unified theorem states $d | n \iff d | (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n \bmod 10))$ whenever $d | (10c - 1)$ and $\gcd(d, 10) = 1$. Proof uses the identity $10(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c(n \bmod 10)) = n + (10c - 1)(n \bmod 10)$ and `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left`.

sections.title: Negative Osculator as Special Case
sections.summary: Derives the negative osculator rule from the unified theorem by substituting -c.
sections.mathContext: If $d | (10c + 1)$, then $d | (10(-c) - 1)$, so the unified theorem with osculator $-c$ gives: $d | n \iff d | (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor - c \cdot (n \bmod 10))$. The sign flip $10(-c) - 1 = -(10c + 1)$ is the key step.

sections.title: Recovering Both Specific Cases
sections.summary: Instantiations for d=7, 11, 13, 17, 19 showing both positive and negative osculator rules recovered from the unified theorem.
sections.mathContext: For each divisor $d \in \{7, 11, 13, 17, 19\}$, the appropriate osculator $c$ is provided and the coprimality/divisibility witnesses are constructed by `decide` and `norm_num`. E.g., $7 | (10 \cdot 2 + 1)$ gives the negative osculator $c = 2$ for divisibility by 7.

sections.title: Dual Osculator Relationship
sections.summary: Theorem: d | (c_pos + c_neg), with verification examples for d=7, 13, 17.
sections.mathContext: Since $10c_+ \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$ and $10c_- \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, we get $10(c_+ + c_-) \equiv 0 \pmod{d}$. Coprimality with 10 then gives $d | (c_+ + c_-)$. For minimal osculators, $c_+ + c_- = d$.

sections.title: Sanity Checks
sections.summary: Numeric examples confirming the rules work: $7 | 49$, $13 | 169$, $19 | 57$, and $\neg(7 | 50)$, all verified by `native_decide`.
sections.mathContext: Sanity checks using `native_decide` for concrete divisibility facts, plus `#check` commands displaying the types of the main theorems.

conclusion.summary: The positive and negative osculator theorems are successfully unified into a single theorem. The key insight is that the negative osculator with parameter c_neg is equivalent to the positive osculator with parameter -c_neg. This reduces the two-theorem framework to a single unified osculator theorem, with the negative case as a one-line corollary. Additionally, the dual osculator sum theorem reveals a structural relationship between the two osculator constants.
conclusion.implications:
This unification:
- **Simplifies the framework**: One theorem instead of two, with the negative case as a corollary
- **Reveals structure**: The dual osculator sum theorem shows c_pos + c_neg is always a multiple of d
- **Confirms universality**: Every divisor coprime to 10 has exactly one osculator up to sign
- **Enables extensions**: The single-theorem framework is easier to generalize to other bases
openQuestions: Can this be extended to divisors that share factors with 10 by combining with the last-k-digits framework?
What is the relationship between the osculator and the continued fraction expansion of 1/d?
Can multi-digit truncation (removing k digits at a time) be unified similarly?
